title: Language and Weather
premise: Theo Montrose has spent five years as a night librarian in a city that never quite sleeps, cataloguing other people's stories while refusing to speak her own—her love for her late mother's caretaker, Wren, and the truth of the name her mother gave her at birth. When a stranger at the funeral addresses the family by that unused name, Theo's careful invisibility collapses, forcing her to confront what her mother hid, why, and what it cost everyone who loved her. As she sorts through her mother's letters in a house being sold out from under her, Theo must choose between the dutiful daughter she performed and the person she actually is. The novel ends with Theo reading her mother's final letter aloud at the graveside, saying both goodbye and her own name for the first time—and asking Wren to stay.
about_author: Felix Sterling is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent a decade cataloguing private letters donated to public collections. Language and Weather is their second novel, written mostly between midnight and dawn.

chapters.title: The Night Shift
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Theo's POV. Theo works the overnight desk at the Halloway Library, shelving returned books and almost texting Wren something true. Establishes her rituals of silence and the city's insomnia. Emotional beat: loneliness mistaken for peace.

chapters.title: The Phone Call at 4 A.M.
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Her brother Marcus calls: their mother, Odile, has died. Theo takes the news with librarian calm, then walks home through rain without an umbrella. Beat: grief arriving as numbness, duty arriving faster than feeling.

chapters.title: A Stranger Knows the Name
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, at the wake. A silver-haired stranger greets the family using 'Vesper'—a name nobody present uses. Theo freezes; the stranger leaves before she can follow. Beat: the first crack in five years of practiced invisibility.

chapters.title: What We Called Each Other
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Theo's POV. Five years earlier: Odile's diagnosis, Wren hired as caretaker, the slow domestic intimacy Theo never named aloud. Beat: tenderness remembered with guilt attached.

chapters.title: Marcus Wants to Sell
chapters.summary: Alternating Theo/Marcus POV. Marcus arrives to empty the house in two weeks; Theo resists, citing unfinished business no one understands. Beat: sibling friction over inheritance as metaphor for competing versions of their mother.

chapters.title: The Locked Drawer
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Sorting Odile's study, Theo finds a locked drawer and a key on a ribbon labeled only 'V.' She doesn't open it yet. Beat: dread braided with longing—the past demanding to be read.

chapters.title: Wren Comes Back
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, first appearance from inside her head. She returns for the funeral's second day, uninvited but unable to stay away. She and Theo circle each other politely, both fluent in avoidance. Beat: love against duty, stated by absence.

chapters.title: Weather Reports
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Intercut with library patrons' small confessions over returned books, Theo recalls how Odile forecast weather like scripture and how the family never discussed anything else. Beat: the theme of unsaid things crystallizing.

chapters.title: The Key Turns
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Alone at night in the house, Theo opens the drawer: letters addressed to Vesper, unsent, decades old—including one revealing Odile changed her daughter's name after a family rupture Theo never knew about. Beat: the ground shifting under her identity.

chapters.title: The Stranger Returns
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The silver-haired woman, Aunt Corliss, appears at the library. She knew Odile before the name change and offers fragments: Odile fled a life, a partner, a self. Beat: inheritance revealed as erasure.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren visits the house to return Odile's medications and nearly tells Theo how she felt during those caretaking years. She leaves without saying it. Beat: two people practicing the same art of almost.

chapters.title: Letters to Vesper
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, epistolary interlude. Theo reads the letters in order across one long night, watching her mother become a whole person she never met. Beat: mourning someone twice—once as mother, once as stranger.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: Dual POV, Theo and Marcus. Theo shows Marcus the letters; he refuses them—his version of Odile cannot survive revision. He sets a hard deadline on the house. Beat: rising tension; belonging offered only on inherited terms.

chapters.title: The City That Sleeps Less
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Insomniac, Theo wanders the pre-dawn city, encountering the library's regulars, each carrying their own unsaid thing. She drafts a resignation letter she doesn't send. Beat: the cost of staying invisible made visible.

chapters.title: Corliss's Story
chapters.summary: Corliss's POV. At a diner, Corliss tells the full story: Odile and Corliss were lovers; when Odile's family threatened to disown her, she chose respectability, took a new surname, named her daughter Vesper as a buried signature. Beat: love against duty, the older generation's version.

chapters.title: What Wren Knew
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren admits she found one letter months ago and said nothing, believing Odile's secrecy was hers to keep. Theo feels betrayed; the argument strips both bare. Beat: climax of interpersonal tension—truth as both wound and gift.

chapters.title: Emptying the House
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Moving day approaches; Theo packs, keeping only the letters and a weather barometer. Marcus and Theo reach a fragile truce—he admits he's afraid too. Beat: grief becoming shared rather than hoarded.

chapters.title: The Last Forecast
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo finds Odile's final letter, dated three days before death, addressed to Vesper: an apology, an instruction to say her own name aloud, and permission to love whoever she chooses. Beat: the emotional keystone; everything converges.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Dual POV, Theo and Wren. A storm knocks power out across the city; Wren comes to the darkened house and they finally say everything—the love, the fear, the years of almost. Beat: climax; confession in candlelight.

chapters.title: Saying Goodbye Properly
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. At the graveside, with Marcus and Corliss present, Theo reads Odile's last letter aloud, then says: 'My name is Vesper Montrose. My mother loved a woman named Corliss. I loved a woman named Wren.' Beat: catharsis; the art of almost ends.

chapters.title: After the Rain
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. The house sells; Vesper keeps her job but changes her name legally, quietly, joyfully. Corliss and Marcus begin their own slow reckonings. Beat: resolution; inheritance reclaimed rather than refused.

chapters.title: Language and Weather
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, closing chapter. Months later, Wren has moved in; they read Odile's letters together on Sunday nights. At the library desk, a patron asks Vesper's name and she answers without flinching. Final beat: belonging chosen, spoken, and kept.
